title: HTTP2_PING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS+HTTP2_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS > 40s will cause all node NotReady
body:
### What happened?

The controller-manager node-lifecycle-controller watches node lease and update `nodeHealthMap` probeTimestamp , and it check node probeTimestamp is before `now - node-monitor-grace-period`. The node-monitor-grace-period default value is 40s.

When the client connection lost, the lease watcher cannot receive new event. With the http2 health check,   HTTP2_PING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS default is 30s, HTTP2_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS default is  15s, it will delay 45s to kill http2  connection.  

During this period, node-lifecycle-controller will mark all nodes NotReady.

Here are some logs

```
I1103 23:00:28.464015       1 node_lifecycle_controller.go:1097] node 10.0.10.240 hasn't been updated for 40.010894415s. Last Ready is: &NodeCondition{Type:Ready,Status:True,LastHeartbeatTime:2023-11-03 22:57:18 +0800 CST,LastTransitionTime:2023-04-21 14:39:17 +0800 CST,Reason:KubeletReady,Message:kubelet is posting ready status,}

W1103 23:00:41.408493       1 reflector.go:441] k8s.io/client-go/informers/factory.go:134: watch of *v1.Lease ended with: an error on the server ("unable to decode an event from the watch stream: http2: client connection lost") has prevented the request from succeeding
```

### What did you expect to happen?

When the http2 connection lost, the watch should stop as soon as possible. The reflector should relist resource, and node-lifecycle-controller should not mark all node NotReady.

HTTP2_PING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS+HTTP2_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS should be less than 40s.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Find the controller-manager node-lifecycle-controller watch client srcIP:srcPort. Drop all tcp package send into srcIP:srcPort.
2. Wait for more than 40 seconds, all node will be marked NotReady
3. All node will be Ready after some seconds.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

I'm investigating problems similar to this, but I'm looking for a way to confirm this is what is happening - and if there are tips for how to recreate such a scenario, that would be very helpful.

We get infrequent reports of "worker goes NotReady for a short time" incidents that appear to be triggered by events like failing over a LB sitting front of the kube-apiservers.

We've done some tests with a simple client-go app and have recreated a scenario in which the app logs `http2: client connection lost` messages after 45 secs of "context exceeded" errors.

The failures reported to us from customers don't have http2 errors in the kubelet logs, and our attempts to recreate with kubelet have never shown more more than a single error which works on subsequent retry.

Hi folks, we have a simulated recreate of the problem. This recreate involves injecting a 40 second delay in "connectivity" between the Kubernetes API server and etcd (we added a 40 second delay to etcd defrag and defragged all etcd members at the same time). The connectivity between these two components is obviously critical to nodes successfully updating their leases in order to stay ready. We use 40 seconds because it matches [Kubernetes etcd keepalive configuration](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/01eb9f47541156a38e4b28759977c06f07f08012/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/storagebackend/factory/etcd3.go#L60-L64). The test will usually cause one or more of the cluster nodes will flap their readiness state. Setting `--node-monitor-grace-period=50s` on the Kubernetes controller manager prevents the flap. Given this, I think that one or more of the Kubernetes default configurations needs to change in order to tolerate such "connectivity" problems in order to maintain healthy node state.
@aojea I think we should update `node-monitor-grace-period`.

> @aojea I think we should update `node-monitor-grace-period`.

can someone send a PR to see how it will look like?

I'll add another data point from our testing. Namely, the simulated recreate noted [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/121793#issuecomment-2239228879) depends on the Kubernetes controller manager (KCM) leader election configuration. Using the following leader election configuration for the KCM yields a KCM that has no leader after the delayed etcd defrag. As a result, nodes won't be marked not ready unless the KCM leadership is restored before the nodes renew their lease.

```
        - --leader-elect-resource-lock=leases
        - --leader-elect=true
        - --leader-elect-renew-deadline=12s
        - --leader-elect-retry-period=3s
```

Extending the KCM leader election configuration to the following, makes the problem easier to recreate.

```
        - --leader-elect-resource-lock=leases
        - --leader-elect=true
        - --leader-elect-lease-duration=137s
        - --leader-elect-renew-deadline=107s
        - --leader-elect-retry-period=26s
```

/assign 
Reassigning the issue to me

Has anyone confirm this issue has been fixed?

I am not convinced that changing it to 50s completely resolved this issue

For example:

00:00 the last successful node HB is served
00:09 the connection becomes stale
00:10 kubelet sends HB
00:20 previous HB is failed with 10s timeout and retry
00:30 failed again and retry
00:40 failed again and retry
00:50 node becomes Unknown
00:54 connection is dropped due to ping timeout (09 + 30 + 15)

this can have an e2e test that shows the problem, it seems it could be also possible to reproduce with an integration test, but we can not keep bumping default values each release https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/127352

nodes.title: hostNetwork pods mount /etc/hosts without network
nodes.body:
/kind bug
Fixes #119852


The kubelet wait for the PodIPs to be present to mount the etc hosts files

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17d7d286201ae4b8e60014d8d0c41792d741d969/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L243-L256

however, it does not check if the pod is host network.

If the Pod is using hostNetwork, then it seems the PodIPs are ignored

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17d7d286201ae4b8e60014d8d0c41792d741d969/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L449-L473

A host network Pod, specially the ones used as static pods, may not have the PodIPs assigned at the star time, but that should not be a dependency for mounting the hosts file, since these pods does not depend on PodIPs for this.

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

hostNetwork pods mount the /etc/hosts from the root namespace, hence does not depend on PodIPs to be populated to mount the /etc/hosts file and add the arguments specified in the Pod.Spec like hostAliases.


```release-note
hostNetwork pods no longer depend on the PodIPs to be assigned to configure the defined hostAliases on the Pod
```

title: Failure to start liveness probe on Windows should be treated like a failed liveness probe
body:
### What happened?

We encountered an issue in our Azure Kubernetes Services clusters on Kubernetes 1.24.9 where, on Windows nodes, Pods came into a state where their liveness probes could no longer be started. Each start of the probe would result in the following error:

> Liveness probe errored: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to exec in container: failed to start exec "d6b7[...]": hcs::System::CreateProcess 05f[...]: The RPC server is unavailable.: unknown

The original reasons of the problem and a memory leak it caused in Windows HCS are discussed elsewhere (e.g., in https://github.com/Azure/AKS/issues/3262 and https://github.com/microsoft/hcsshim/issues/1680), but I'd like to discuss a different issue here: Kubernetes did not treat these _failures to start the liveness probes_ the same way it treats _failed liveness probes_. And I think it should have, because this way, we had to monitor and restart the Pods ourselves.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect that Kubernetes treats a _failure to start a liveness probe_ the same way it treats a _failed liveness probe_. I.e., consider the Pod unhealthy and restart it. This would contribute to the self-healing of the system.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Unfortunately, I do not have a simple repro for this issue. One needs to, on a Windows node:
* have a Pod with a command liveness probe,
* get the Pod into a state where the _CExecSvc_ within the container can no longer respond to the containerd instructions to create the process (=> _"The RPC server is unavailable"_),
* then observe how the Pod is not considered unhealthy and restarted as it would be if the liveness probe _failed_.

### Anything else we need to know?

It might be the error is in _hcshim_ or _containerd_ rather than the parts of Kubernetes covered in this repository.  If so, please do tell me and I will raise the issue in the correct repository.

title: PV handling of beta topology labels
body:
### What happened?

Offshoot discussion from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114120 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/89477

There has been a lot of work since 1.14 to start using the GA topology labels instead of the beta topology labels.

The intree volume provisioning logic has been updated to create PVs with the GA topology labels (both as a label, and in PV.NodeAffinity) and the CSI migration library has been updated to understand both beta and GA labels and convert them in-memory to the CSI equivalent labels in order to support old PVs with only beta labels: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/98281

However, there's still a few gaps:
1. The CSI migration logic only handles conversion of the beta labels for intree volume types. External volume types are not covered.
2. The [VolumeZone](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumezone) scheduling plugin does not exercise the csi migration logic. The original plan was that with csi migration we could remove the VolumeZone plugin entirely because its functionality is replaced by the [VolumeBinding](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding) plugin. Again, this assumption is only true for intree volume types that we provision and does not account for users that may have their own custom provisioning logic.

These issues mean that if we remove the beta label on nodes, we can break existing PVs that only use the beta label, for both intree and external volume types.


### What did you expect to happen?

There's a couple of options (not necessarily mutually exclusive) that we can pursue:
1. Anywhere we look at PV labels (scheduler, kubelet), translate beta labels to GA labels in-memory regardless of csi migration. This method requires the fewest user changes but since the object itself is not changed, users may still see warnings about use of the beta labels.
2. Relax PV.NodeAffinity mutability to allow changing the beta label to GA label (changing PV.Labels should already be allowed). And then
    a. Require the user to change all the labels themselves. This is quite burdensome but gives the user the most control over when and how to change it.
    b. Provide tooling/controller that updates all the objects. Convenient, but could possibly break the user if they had tooling/workflows that were depending on the beta label.
3. Never remove the beta topology label from the node and continue supporting it forever. Similar to how we say beta annotations are part of the API, and stable APIs are supported forever: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/deprecation-policy/#deprecating-parts-of-the-api

I think we should do some form of option 2 regardless.

If 3 is out of the question, then I would say 1 + 2a, which gives us the benefit removing the label from nodes and letting users convert on their own time. But this would probably apply more to just PVs; anywhere we allow users to specify the labels needs to be able to handle this.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Remove the beta zone label on a Node and try to schedule a Pod using PV.labels with the beta zone label.

Do we have a concrete list of all the types / fields and controllers that use node labels / selectors / affinity? That seems like the starting point for any of the options. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/94626 did a sweep a few releases back, but was focused just on the API aspect, not on consuming controllers. There's enough types and enough clients/controllers looking at those types that are outside the core Kubernetes components that I tend to think putting a translation layer in the controllers is probably not going to work well.

I agree with this.
I may have been a little vague in my last comment.  I mean we can postpone the removal of the deprecated fields until we can. I don't mean we should remove it even if it will break users.

My main concern is that there is always a risk of breaking unknown consumers despite all the warnings that we give. Should we adopt the same API deprecation policy as beta annotations for our well-known labels?

I'm not sure we should commit to keeping the beta labels forever until we've ruled out a way to transition existing uses seamlessly, but if we cannot transition existing uses seamlessly, I would consider it.
For the page https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/, I've assumed that we will always retain the _registration_ for deprecated labels indefinitely, once registered.

could be out-of-tree, and we can put a big notice in the release notes saying:
- release n: *go and run this tool (or controller Deployment) if you have beta topology keys*

title: Misintepretation of integer-like strings when deploying a ConfigMap
body:
### What happened?

Example working config map:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: game-demo
data:
  shortCommitHash: '0340914'
```

example of failing config map:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: game-demo
data:
  shortCommitHash: 0340914
```
The difference is missing quotes around the value of shortCommitHash parameter.
The error is quite descriptive: "Invalid value: "map[data:map[shortCommitHash:340914]]": cannot convert int64 to string"
However this int-looking value according to [yaml specification](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#10213-integer) is not really an int, because it does not match a pattern (as it starts with 0). In fact its is a string. 
This happens to cause problems when using libraries like SnakeYaml for Java, which seem to correctly bypass quotes for a value like that, because according to the Yaml specification it should be implicitly considered a string and quotes are not necessary. Therefore when we use SnakeYaml library to prepare deployment Yaml files and then try to deploy those files to Kubernetes the process fails.

### What did you expect to happen?

ConfigMap should be considered valid even without quotes

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

As described above

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_
